---
title: "Using Models Well"
subtitle: "Turning what the course has taught into working habits: task selection, context, tools, verification, and knowing when to stop"
---

*Prerequisites: none strictly, but this page assumes the mental model
that `short-story.qmd` gives in ten minutes and that the lessons develop
in full: a model predicts tokens from a finite context; training set its
parameters; tools and loops around it can act on the world. Each claim
below links to the page that establishes it.*

## The central principle

Good model use is not mainly about clever wording. It is about choosing
an appropriate task; supplying the right evidence and context; specifying
what success looks like; giving the system useful tools where the answer
depends on the world; making important outputs observable and
verifiable; and keeping a human responsible for the judgments that the
checks cannot settle. Every one of those follows from a mechanism the
course has already explained, and this page develops them as concrete
decisions rather than as a slogan. [S-63]

## 1. Start with task selection

Before writing anything, decide what kind of task this is, because the
kind determines what the model's output is worth on its own. Three
categories cover most work.

**Tasks where the output is useful as a draft or transformation.**
Summarizing supplied material, restructuring text, explaining a concept,
brainstorming options, drafting or rewriting, translating, extracting
structured information from a document, and generating a bounded piece
of code or a formula that can be checked. These are often useful places
to begin because the output is directly reviewable or can be compared
with the supplied material. The output is not automatically correct, and
errors in a summary, a translation, an extraction, a formula, or a piece
of code can be subtle; factual or technical claims in it may still
require verification. The point of the category is that the output is
useful as a draft or transformation, not that its mistakes are obvious.

**Tasks that become strong with tools and verification.** Research that
depends on current sources, calculations, code modification, data
analysis, work across many files, checking a product or documentation
fact, and multi-step repository work. What these share is that a tool
can retrieve the evidence or make success observable: a search can fetch
the source, a script can compute the number, a test can run. Without the
tool, the model is asked to guess what could have been observed. With it,
the loop `learn/agents.qmd` describes can close on evidence.

**Tasks that should not be treated as an unreviewed final decision.**
Consequential factual conclusions without source checking; high-stakes
professional decisions; irreversible external actions; research-design
judgments; causal interpretation; and any decision where the model lacks
essential private or current information. The model can assist with all
of these, often substantially, by organizing the evidence, surfacing
considerations, or drafting the argument. What it cannot do is remove
the need for a person or an external source to settle the answer,
because nothing in the training objective verified truth
(`learn/training.qmd` §7) and nothing in a fluent answer indicates that
it was checked. [S-08]

## 2. A prompt is a task specification

There is no magic phrasing. What makes a request work is that it
specifies a task the way you would specify it for a capable colleague who
knows nothing about your situation. A useful specification says some or
all of the following: the objective; the source of truth; the inputs;
the relevant context; the constraints; the required output; the
acceptance criteria; and what to do when evidence is missing or the
request is ambiguous. Not every task needs every part. Precision comes
from defining the task, not from length.

Compare two versions of one request.

> "Review this analysis and tell me if it is right."

This gives the model no source of truth, no definition of "right", no
list of what to check, and no instruction for the case where a claim
cannot be established. The model can still produce a plausible-looking
review even though the task was underspecified, and fluency does not
establish that the review is correct.

> "Review the analysis in `report.md`, treating the attached data file
> as the source of truth. Identify assumptions the text relies on
> without support. Recompute the three figures in Table 2 from the data
> and report any mismatch. Return findings ordered by severity. Do not
> fill gaps with invented evidence; if a conclusion cannot be
> established from the supplied material, say so and stop there."

This is four sentences longer and specifies everything the first version
left open: what to inspect, what counts as truth, which numbers to
recompute, what form the answer takes, and what to do at the boundary of
the evidence. Anthropic's current guidance for its models makes the same
point in its own terms: clear, explicit instructions, with the context
and motivation behind them, produce more targeted responses. [S-57] The
principle is older than any model, since it is how tasks are specified
for people, and it is stable across providers in a way that phrasing
tricks are not (§9).

## 3. Context engineering

A model step is shaped by its learned parameters and by the
inference-time context supplied to that step. Surrounding software and
tools can retrieve or observe external information and place the
relevant results into later context. `learn/tokens-context.qmd` explains
the window: finite, holding instructions, conversation, supplied files,
tool results, and generated output together. [S-31] Managing what goes
into it is the practical skill the industry has come to call **context
engineering**, and the question it asks for every step is simple: what
information actually needs to be in context now?

The guiding principle is the smallest high-signal context that is
sufficient for the next step. Supplying everything is not the safe
default it appears to be. The window is finite, so material that is not
needed displaces material that is. Irrelevant content competes with
relevant content; one empirical study found that models used a relevant
passage less well when it sat in the middle of a long input, and
Anthropic's documentation states that as token count grows, accuracy and
recall degrade, and that context should be treated as a finite resource.
[S-32] [S-31] [S-34] Those are findings for particular models and dates
rather than laws, but the direction is consistent: more is not
automatically better. Repeated material occupies capacity twice, and
additional input consumes context capacity and computation; depending on
the product, API, pricing, and caching scheme, it can also increase
latency or monetary cost (§11).

Several practices follow. Separate durable project instructions, which
apply to every task, from task-specific instructions, which apply to
this one; keep the durable set short, since instructions that are always
loaded compete with everything else. Load a file or a section when the
step needs it rather than at the start of the session, a pattern
Anthropic's engineering guidance calls **just-in-time** context: the
system keeps lightweight references such as file paths or queries and
loads the data at runtime with tools, so that what it discovers at each
step informs the next, which the same guidance calls **progressive
disclosure**. [S-61] Retrieve the relevant part of an archive rather
than pasting the archive. Remove context that has become stale or is
duplicated. When a long session becomes unwieldy, summarize its state
into a compact form and continue from that, which is called
**compaction** when the system does it automatically and a **handoff**
when you do it deliberately (§8). [S-61] And when the existing history
is more noise than signal, start a fresh session with a clean
specification. These are general practices; how a particular product
implements loading, compaction, or memory is product-specific and
changes.

## 4. The source-of-truth question

Before asking for an answer, decide where the answer should come from.
The candidates are the model's general knowledge from training; a
document you supply; current web sources; a database; code you run; a
spreadsheet; a repository; or a connected application. The choice is
not a formality. A model's parameters encode statistical regularities
from training text, not a queryable record of your document, your
database, or last week's release notes, and a model asked a question
whose answer lives elsewhere will produce a plausible continuation
anyway. [S-08]

Three examples fix the habit. If the question is "What does this
contract say?", the contract is the source of truth, and it must be in
context; the model's general knowledge of contracts is background, not
evidence. If the question is "What is the current version of this
software?", current documentation is the source of truth, and the answer
should be fetched, not recalled, because the parameters were fixed at
training time and the world was not. If the question is "Does this code
produce the claimed number?", running the code or recomputing the number
is the source of truth, and any answer that did not involve running or
recomputing is a guess about what running it would show. Deciding the
source first tells you what to put in context and whether a tool is
needed, which is the next section.

## 5. Give the model tools when the answer depends on the world

A model can reason about what is in its context. A tool is needed when
the task depends on something that is not there and cannot be there
without an action: current information, private data, exact arithmetic
beyond what should be trusted from token prediction, the contents of a
file, the result of executing code, or a real effect on an external
system. `learn/agents.qmd` §2 explains what a tool call is: the model
generates a structured request, and surrounding software executes it and
returns the result as evidence for the next step. [S-51]

The pairing is usually obvious once the source of truth is named. A web
search or fetch for current information; retrieval for a document
collection; a Python or R execution tool for calculations; file-system
tools for files; a test runner for code; a database query for what is
actually stored. The principle that covers every case is short: do not
ask a model to guess what a tool can observe. Where no tool is available
for something the task depends on, the honest specification says so and
tells the model to state the gap rather than fill it.

## 6. Verification: evidence beats confidence

A fluent answer is not evidence. A sentence saying "I checked" is still
generated output; by itself it does not establish that the check was
executed or what the check found. What counts is observable
verification: something outside the model's generated text that a
person, or a later step, can inspect. A calculation independently recomputed by a
script; a test suite run, with its output shown; a rendered document
opened; a quotation checked against the original; a database queried; an
output validated against a schema; the version-control diff read; every
claim reconciled against its cited source. Anthropic's current guidance
for its coding tool states the working rule bluntly: have the model show
evidence rather than asserting success, and if you cannot verify it, do
not ship it. [S-60]

The standing rule of this course applies to every such check: a passing
check establishes only what that check tested. That limit divides
verification into two kinds. **Mechanical verification** covers what a
procedure can settle: arithmetic, syntax, whether a document renders,
whether tests pass, whether a file exists, whether output matches a
schema. It is cheap, repeatable, and should be built into any task that
admits it. **Judgment** covers what no procedure settles: whether a
research design identifies the effect it claims to, whether the evidence
supports the conclusion, whether the specification itself was right,
whether a piece of prose argues fairly. Automation can support judgment,
by assembling the evidence and running every mechanical check first, but
it does not eliminate it. A task that passes every automated check has
passed every automated check, and the question of whether the right
thing was built remains open until someone answers it.

## 7. Long tasks: work in bounded units

A request such as "do the entire project" asks for one very large,
opaque task, and that makes the intermediate decisions harder to inspect,
verify, and redirect before they affect later work; meanwhile the context
fills with every file read and every command run along the way. The
alternative is the pattern that agent systems
already use internally, made explicit at the level of your own
workflow: inspect the current state; plan the next bounded unit;
execute it; run the checks; review the diff or output; record the
decisions made; continue. Each pass through that sequence is a point
where you can see what happened and redirect. Anthropic's guidance for
its coding tool recommends the same separation of exploration and
planning from implementation, and notes that planning pays most when
the approach is uncertain or the change spans many files, and least when
the change could be described in one sentence. [S-60]

A good bounded unit has a clear deliverable, an explicit scope in files
or sections, acceptance checks that can be run, and a stop condition.
For file-based work, a checkpoint in version control at the end of each
unit gives you a known-good state to compare against and return to;
reviewing the diff between checkpoints is often the fastest way to see
exactly what a unit changed. This is not a tutorial on version control,
and the mechanism does not matter; what matters is that every unit ends
in a state you have looked at.

## 8. Handoffs and fresh sessions

Long work outgrows a single session, and switching sessions or models is
routine. A good handoff preserves the objective; the current state; the
decisions already settled, so they are not relitigated; the files and
the source of truth; the open issues; the next bounded task; and what
must not be changed. It does not preserve the transcript. A compact
state summary is usually better than the history it summarizes, because
the history contains every dead end, every superseded draft, and every
tool result that no longer matters.

That is also why a fresh session can sometimes be preferable. There is
nothing mystical in it: irrelevant accumulated context can interfere
with the next task, and a compact handoff into a fresh context removes it
and lets the next task be specified cleanly. Anthropic's current guidance
for Claude Code, accessed 2026-09-15, gives a concrete trigger for that
product: if the model has been corrected more than twice on the same
issue in one session, the context is cluttered with failed approaches,
and a clean session with a better initial prompt that incorporates what
was learned almost always outperforms the long one. [S-60] That is one
provider's rule of thumb for one tool, not a law of language models; the
durable principle is only the one in the first sentence of this
paragraph. A handoff can be as short as this:

```
Objective: <one sentence>
State: <what exists now, which checks pass, which files are current>
Settled: <decisions not to reopen, with one-line reasons>
Source of truth: <files, data, documentation, with locations>
Open: <known problems, unverified items>
Next unit: <deliverable, scope, acceptance checks, stop condition>
Do not change: <frozen files, constraints>
```

## 9. Prompting guidance is conditional, not folklore

Prompting advice circulates as if it were a fixed craft. It is not. The
official guidance of the major providers, read on the same day, differs
on specific recommendations, and each provider's guidance is explicitly
tied to particular models and dates. The examples below were verified
against those documents on 2026-09-15 and will go stale; they are here
to show the pattern, not to be memorized.

On examples in prompts, three current documents give three different
defaults. Anthropic's prompting-best-practices page, which covers its
current Claude models and separates model-specific guidance from
techniques it applies to all of them, lists examples among the
techniques for all current models, calls them one of the most reliable
ways to steer output format, tone, and structure, and suggests three to
five. [S-57] Google's current Gemini prompt-design guidance recommends
always including few-shot examples and states that prompts without them
are likely to be less effective. [S-59] OpenAI's guidance is split by
model family: its reasoning-models guide says those models often do not
need few-shot examples and recommends writing prompts without examples
first, while its general prompt-engineering page says its non-reasoning
GPT models perform best with explicit instructions. [S-58] On
step-by-step instructions, the same OpenAI reasoning-models guide says
that prompting those models to think step by step is unnecessary because
they reason internally, and Anthropic's page, in its section on
extended thinking, says that when thinking is enabled a general
instruction to think thoroughly often produces better reasoning than a
hand-written step-by-step plan, while keeping manual step-by-step
prompting as a fallback when thinking is off. [S-58] [S-57] On structure,
Anthropic's page and OpenAI's general prompt-engineering page both
recommend delimiting the parts of a prompt with XML tags or Markdown so
that instructions, context, and inputs are unambiguous. [S-57] [S-58] On
a specific mechanism, prefilling the start of the assistant's reply to
force a format, Anthropic's page states that it is no longer supported on
its models from Claude 4.6 onward and gives migration advice. [S-57] And
OpenAI's prompt-engineering page recommends pinning production
applications to specific model snapshots precisely because behavior
changes between versions. [S-58]

The conclusion is not that any of these is wrong. It is that
model-specific guidance can conflict, so prompting advice is model-,
task-, and date-dependent and should be treated that way: verify the
current guidance for the model you are using rather than memorizing
syntax tricks, try the simplest specification first, and add structure or
examples when the output shows they are needed. What does not change between models or
years is the content of §2: a clear objective, the relevant context, a
named source of truth, and acceptance criteria that can be checked. Those
are properties of the task, and they outlast every syntax trick.

## 10. Model and effort selection

Providers offer models of different sizes and, increasingly, settings
that control how much computation a model spends before answering. The
right choice depends on where the difficulty in the task lies, and the
following is a heuristic rather than an empirical law. Judgment-heavy,
ambiguous, multi-source, or technically difficult work, such as
synthesis across many sources, difficult debugging, complex planning, or
subtle technical writing, is a reasonable candidate for a stronger model
or higher reasoning effort, especially when mistakes are costly. Bounded
and mechanically checkable work, such as transformations, repetitive
structured tasks, mechanical edits, checks, and simple classification or
extraction, is a reasonable candidate for a faster or cheaper model,
whose lower cost and latency are paid on every call. OpenAI's current
guidance draws a similar line for its own model families: speed and cost
favor one, accuracy and reliability on hard problems favor the other.
[S-58] Evaluate the trade-off on the actual task when it matters; model
capabilities and pricing change.

No universal ranking by model name survives contact with a specific task,
and any such ranking is out of date within months. The durable
principle is to match model capability and inference effort to the
difficulty and value of the decision, rather than always choosing either
the strongest or the cheapest option.

## 11. Token and cost efficiency

In ordinary interactive use, you do not need to count tokens. A few
habits cover most of the waste: do not supply the same long material
repeatedly across turns; keep instructions to what the task needs; ask
for bounded outputs rather than open-ended ones; and start fresh when the
accumulated context no longer helps (§8). Efficiency here is a by-product
of the context discipline in §3, not a separate goal.

In API and agent workflows, cost and latency deserve attention, for
structural reasons. The context may be sent with every call, and a tool
loop makes many calls; long outputs accumulate into later inputs;
stronger models and higher effort cost more per token. One mechanism
that helps is **prompt caching**, in which a provider stores a repeated
prefix of the input so that it is cheaper and faster to process on later
calls. It should be understood precisely: Anthropic's documentation
states that cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window, and
that caching changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they
count. [S-62] Caching lowers the bill for repeated material; it does not
make the material free in the sense that matters for §3. And no
efficiency measure is worth a wrong answer: when correctness and cost
conflict, the section on verification wins.

## 12. When to stop and ask

A capable system should not always continue. There are situations in
which the right next action is to stop and ask, and a task specification
should name them: the source of truth is missing; the action has
meaningful external consequences; two plausible interpretations of the
request would lead to materially different work; required access is
unavailable; a requested acceptance criterion cannot be checked; the
evidence contradicts the conclusion that was requested. In each, an
uncertainty should change the workflow, not merely the wording of the
answer. A hedged answer to an ambiguous request still does the wrong
work confidently; a question resolves the ambiguity before the work is
done.

The counterweight is that routine tasks should not become
interruptive. Most small ambiguities do not matter: either reading leads
to the same result, or the difference is cheap to fix on review. The
practical test is whether the ambiguity materially affects correctness or
consequences. If it does, stopping is cheaper than proceeding. If it does
not, a stated assumption and a note in the result is enough.

## 13. Privacy, permissions, and consequential actions

Before giving a model or an agent access to sensitive files, private
accounts, external communication, production systems, or destructive
commands, decide what access the task actually needs. `learn/agents.qmd`
§10 explains where boundaries live: in the software around the model,
which decides what executes automatically, what waits for approval, and
what is refused, regardless of what the model generates. [S-54] The
principle is least necessary access, with review for consequential
actions. Local, reversible, observable actions are often easier to permit
than irreversible or externally consequential ones, but risk also depends
on what data and systems an action can access: reading can be
consequential when the source is sensitive, confidential, or restricted.
Actions that send, publish, delete, pay, change production systems, or
expose sensitive information commonly warrant explicit review at the
point of execution. The same holds for what you place in context:
sensitive material should be supplied only when the service, account,
organizational policy, and data-handling terms permit that use. This is
not a security manual, only the habit of asking, before each task, what
the system is being allowed to touch.

## 15. Check your understanding

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>You ask a model, from general knowledge, what the current
default context-window size of a particular product is. It answers
confidently with a number. What is wrong with this workflow?</summary>
The source of truth for a current product fact is current documentation,
not the model's parameters, which were fixed at training time. The
answer is a plausible continuation, and its confidence is not evidence.
The task needed a fetch of the documentation, or an explicit statement
that the model cannot know (§4–§5).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>To be safe, you paste your entire project archive into the
context before asking a question about one function. Why might this
produce a worse answer than supplying the one relevant file?</summary>
The window is finite, and unneeded material competes with needed
material; the empirical and vendor evidence cited in §3 points the same
way. Supplying the relevant file, or letting a tool retrieve it, gives a
smaller, higher-signal context for the same question (§3).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>An agent reports: "I have fixed the bug and verified that the
tests pass." What have you learned, and what should you look at?</summary>
You have learned that the model generated that sentence. Look at the
test output the run actually produced, and at the diff. If no test was
run through a tool, nothing was verified. If it was, the passing tests
establish what those tests check, and whether the fix is right in the
sense you meant remains your judgment (§6).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>You use the cheapest, fastest model to decide whether a
research design supports a causal claim, to save cost. What is the
mismatch?</summary>
The bottleneck in that task is judgment and synthesis, and the cost of
error is high, which makes it a candidate for stronger or higher-effort
assistance plus human review, not for the cheapest option. Cost saving
belongs on the bounded, mechanically checkable parts of a workflow. And
whatever model is used, this is a task that stays under human judgment;
the model's role is to organize the evidence (§1, §10).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>You want an agent to migrate a large codebase. Which is the
better first request: "migrate the whole codebase" or "migrate the three
files in `src/io/`, run the test suite, and stop; report what changed"?
</summary>
The second. It has a deliverable, an explicit scope, an acceptance check,
and a stop condition, so you can review the diff and the test output
before the next unit. The first is one opaque pass whose early mistakes
shape everything after them (§7).
</details>
:::

::: {.check-understanding}
<details>
<summary>After the third correction on the same point, the assistant is
still getting it wrong. Should you correct it a fourth time?</summary>
That is a reasonable point to consider a fresh session or a handoff,
especially if the accumulated history now contains several failed
approaches competing with the task. The exact number is a heuristic, not
a fixed threshold. The durable principle is to start fresh, with a
specification that includes what you learned from the failures, when
accumulated context is adding more noise than useful state (§8).
</details>
:::

## 16. Continue learning

- **Anthropic, *Effective context engineering for AI agents***
  (engineering article, published 2025-09-29, accessed 2026-09-15).
  Practitioner level. The clearest statement of context as a finite
  resource, with definitions of just-in-time retrieval, compaction, and
  structured note-taking used in §3. Limitation: one provider's guidance
  about its own models; the mechanisms it names are implemented
  differently elsewhere.
  <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents>

- **Anthropic, *Best practices for Claude Code*** (documentation page,
  accessed 2026-09-15). Practitioner level. Especially good on
  verification as the thing that lets a session run unattended, on
  separating exploration from implementation, and on when to clear
  context. Limitation: product-specific; the habits transfer, the
  commands do not.
  <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices>

- **The three providers' current prompting guidance** (Anthropic's
  *Prompting best practices*; OpenAI's *Prompt engineering* and
  *Reasoning best practices*; Google's *Prompt design strategies*; all
  accessed 2026-09-15). Practitioner level. Read the one for the model
  you use, and read it again when the model changes. Limitation: each is
  tied to its provider's current models and revised without notice, which
  is the point of §9.
  <https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices>,
  <https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering>,
  <https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies>

See `resources.qmd` for the complete list of sources used across this
